limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that the results depend entirely on obtaining histologically free resection margins, that extensive preoperative and perioperative assessment is needed so that inappropriate extensive resection is avoided, that prospective studies of preoperative biliary drainage in obstructive jaundice have failed to show significant overall benefit although they still use it in selected cases, and that published results of transplantation for this disease have generally been poor with a high incidence of recurrence
critique: Twenty-three resections accumulated over thirty years at one centre, during which imaging, staging and operative technique changed completely; the type-specific operative recommendations rest on one to four patients per tumour type, and the type IV recommendation of transplantation on three patients, one of whom recurred in the hepatic pedicle 8 months after transplantation
No statistical comparison of any kind appears in the paper: no P value, no log-rank test and no confidence interval, so the claim that group C outcomes exceeded groups A and B is purely descriptive

Three different counts are given for the same set of potentially curative resections: 7 patients with two type I lesions in the abstract, 8 patients with three type I lesions in the Results and Discussion, and 9 patients in group C in Table 2

The 70-year-old patient with a papillary tumour who survived 11 years free of recurrence was removed from the survival analysis as atypical after her outcome was known, while remaining the case that supports the abstract's recommendation of local excision for type I disease; she is 71 in Table 1 and 70 in the text

The claim that local recurrence was never observed when the margin was histologically free is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1 and Results, where two group C patients died of recurrence at 14 and 22 months, one of them with recurrence at the anastomosis and in the hepatic pedicle at 10 months

Operative mortality is reported as zero with mortality defined as death during or within two months of surgery, a window wider than the conventional 30 or 90 days; zero events in 23 patients carries an upper confidence bound near 15%

There is no comparison group: patients treated by surgical bypass or transtumoral intubation were never analysed, only 23 of 122 operated patients were resected, and the survival credited to margin-negative resection is uncontrolled and heavily selected

Group B is defined as microscopic tumour at the resection margin or lymph nodes outside the hepatic pedicle, so margin status and nodal status are mixed in one group and the margin effect is not isolated

Figure 1, showing operative type IV rising from 4 to 9 on postoperative histology, includes the 3 transplanted patients and so counts 26 cases, while the survival analysis excludes them and counts 23, so classification accuracy and outcome are computed on different denominators

Follow-up averaged 26 months with a minimum of 6, and 10 patients were still alive at 6 to 48 months, so the 3-year figures of 25% overall survival and 50% in group C rest on almost no patients still at risk, with no numbers at risk given anywhere

Caudate resection was performed in only 8 of the 13 liver resections, yet the recommendation is that every type II to IV lesion requires it; that recommendation rests on Nimura's anatomical argument rather than on any comparison within this series

Table 3's assessment of curability excludes the 4 patients with gross residual tumour and 3 with distant nodal disease, leaving 16 patients from whom the entire type-specific operative algorithm is derived

Ten of the 23 patients (43%) had already undergone surgical drainage or transtumoral intubation elsewhere and all but 5 had been investigated or treated at another institution, so this is a referred, pre-treated population
Preoperative percutaneous drainage is endorsed for selected cases while the paper itself cites two prospective studies showing no benefit, and only one patient in the series actually received it

Denominators shift between the 136 consecutive patients, the 122 taken to surgery and the 23 resected, with the 19% resectability rate and the 15.6% and 7.4% curative resection rates all computed on 122
No chemotherapy, radiotherapy or adjuvant treatment data are reported for any patient, and causes of death are not tabulated
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
1309988.n: 23 resections for hilar cholangiocarcinoma performed between January 1960 and December 1990 at one Paris centre, drawn from 136 consecutive patients of whom 122 were considered suitable for surgical treatment, with 3 further patients treated by total hepatectomy and transplantation excluded from the outcome analysis
1309988.bottom_line: This is the source of the modified Bismuth-Corlette classification and of the type-driven operation: local excision for type I, with caudate resection added for type II, with right or left hepatectomy for type III, and transplantation considered for type IV. It rests on 23 resections over thirty years at one centre, one to four patients per type, no comparison group, no statistical test of any kind, and a classification the paper itself shows is unreliable before operation, four operative type IV lesions becoming nine on histology. What it establishes is that margin clearance rather than nodal status drove outcome in this series and that achieving it requires the hepatectomy the anatomy dictates; the survival figures and the type IV recommendation should not be carried forward.
1309988.funding: No funding statement and no declaration of interests anywhere in the paper

limitations: No limitations section; the authors state 'We acknowledge difficulties in comparing results between the resection and transplant groups' and then set out the selection asymmetry: the transplant group was significantly younger with higher rates of primary sclerosing cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease, by protocol design no transplant recipient had regional nodal metastases, medical selection criteria were more stringent for transplantation while tumour selection criteria were less stringent, and none of the transplant patients was a candidate for resection

Rosen concedes in the published discussion that the age difference between the groups is difficult to correct for, and that removing the patients with sclerosing cholangitis only partly corrects for it

Eight of the 38 recipients had no histological or cytological confirmation of carcinoma before neoadjuvant therapy; the authors note that one might be sceptical of those diagnoses and report that omitting them changes 5-year survival from 82% to 80%

The change in the timing of staging laparotomy in 2002, from near the time of transplantation to immediately after brachytherapy, may lower the yield of staging and allow disease progression to go undetected, leading to more recurrence after transplantation, which the authors state as an explicit concern
The most serious disadvantage of the protocol is the limitation of donor organ availability

The appealed MELD score of 20 was, in Rosen's own words in the discussion, an arbitrary decision agreed locally with the only other liver programme in the organ procurement organisation, and neither the correct starting point nor the correct increment is known
Transplantation becomes technically more difficult the longer a patient waits after neoadjuvant therapy and staging, with portal vein stenosis and friable tissues attributed to the radiation
critique: The two survival curves start at different points. The 82% figure is survival from transplantation among the 38 who survived neoadjuvant therapy, staging and the waiting list, while 33 of the 71 enrolled never reached transplantation; the 21% figure is survival from operation among the 26 of 54 resected. From the start of treatment the comparison is 58% against about 21%, and Figure 1 is the only near-intention-to-treat comparison the paper offers

The best-selected resection subgroup did worse, not better: the node-negative margin-negative resections had 5-year survival of 18% against 21% for the whole resection group, which undercuts the argument that nodal and margin selection explains the gap

No statistical adjustment of any kind is attempted. The comparison is a log-rank test on unmatched groups differing by 15 years of mean age, by aetiology (22 of 38 transplant recipients had primary sclerosing cholangitis against 2 of 26 resections) and by protocol-mandated nodal status

Protocol exclusions make the groups non-exchangeable by construction: prior attempted resection or operative biopsy of the tumour barred a patient from the transplant arm, so patients who had been explored are structurally in the resection group

Five of the 71 protocol patients (7%) died during neoadjuvant therapy, four of sepsis and one of pulmonary embolism, and four more progressed beyond transplant criteria; none of this treatment-related mortality appears in the post-transplant curve that carries the paper's claim

Internal inconsistencies are not reconciled: the Results state that 8 of the 16 explants without residual tumour had unequivocal preoperative confirmation while the Discussion states 9 and refers to 'the other 7'; the node-negative margin-negative resection group is 15 patients in the Results and 16 in the Discussion and Figure 4; and 5-year survival after resection is 21% in the abstract and 20% in the Discussion

Sixteen of 38 explants (42%) contained no residual tumour, and from 2003 a CA 19-9 above 100 or digital image analysis or FISH aneuploidy alone sufficed for enrolment, so some transplanted patients may never have had cancer; Roberts raised exactly this point in the published discussion

Recurrence is compared as crude percentages, 13% against 27%, and mean time to recurrence as 40 against 21 months, although the transplant group's clock starts later and the follow-up durations of the two groups are never compared

At censoring one patient awaited staging and nine awaited transplantation; all are inside the 71-patient denominator of the intention-to-treat curve with minimal follow-up, and no numbers at risk appear on any figure

The comparator operation is not maximal by the paper's own standards: left hepatectomy in 13 of 26, extended right hepatectomy in only 1, and caudate resection in only 10 of 26 (38%), against the Neuhaus series quoted in the Discussion reporting 72% 5-year survival after margin-negative right trisegmentectomy with portal vein resection

Thirty-day mortality after resection was 12% (3 of 26), and Wall observes in the discussion that recurrence after resection was only about 30% while 5-year survival was 20%, implying that non-cancer deaths drive much of the difference

Seven living donor grafts were used and two of the three surgical deaths in the transplant arm followed living donor transplantation, yet no donor morbidity or mortality is reported and the organ cost of 38 grafts for 71 enrolled patients is never discussed

Twenty-three percent of patients taken to staging had findings precluding transplantation, but that yield is not stable across the study: before 2002 staging was done near the time of transplantation and nearly 40% of early patients had positive findings, while after the 2002 change very few did, so the single 23% figure spans two different practices
The CA 19-9 diagnostic criterion is reported in ng/mL rather than U/mL throughout

The published discussion (Ann Surg 2005;242:458-61) records the substantive objections: Roberts on diagnostic certainty in primary sclerosing cholangitis and on explant pathology, Shaw on the limited selection and the radiation dose, Wall on non-cancer mortality in the resected group, and Jenkins on how to counsel a non-PSC patient when the transplant results are set against resection results that every centre achieves
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
16135931.n: 71 patients with unresectable hilar cholangiocarcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma arising in primary sclerosing cholangitis enrolled in the Mayo neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplant protocol between January 1993 and August 2004, of whom 38 were transplanted, compared with 54 patients explored for potentially curative resection over the same period, of whom 26 were resected
16135931.bottom_line: This is the Mayo single-centre report that put neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by transplantation on the map, with 82% 5-year survival after transplantation against 21% after resection. The two figures are not comparable: by protocol no transplant patient was resectable and every recipient was proved node-negative at staging laparotomy, while 31% of resections were node-positive and 12% margin-positive, and the transplant curve starts at transplantation although 33 of 71 enrolled patients never got there, so from the start of treatment the comparison is 58% against about 21%. The defensible claim is what the protocol achieves in a selected, node-negative, mostly PSC population, in which 16 of 38 explants held no residual tumour and 8 recipients had no tissue proof of cancer.
16135931.funding: No funding statement and no declaration of interests anywhere in the paper or the published discussion

limitations: A primary weakness is that the groups were not randomised, although the authors state there were no remarkable demographic differences between them

The study is limited by its retrospective nature, and the authors judge that a prospective randomised trial comparing transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration with other diagnostic methods is unlikely to be feasible because the diagnosis is infrequent and patients ineligible for curative therapy may die before peritoneal seeding becomes clinically evident
The overall number of patients undergoing transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration is small, with six in the biopsy-positive group

Information such as tumour differentiation or perineural invasion was not known at enrolment given the limited amount of diagnostic tissue, so the groups could not be matched on the histological features that predict peritoneal spread

The reason the incidence of peritoneal seeding here exceeds that reported after percutaneous cholangiography and after fine-needle aspiration for hepatocellular carcinoma is unknown; the explanations offered, greater peritoneal exposure and relative immunosuppression after chemoradiotherapy, are hypotheses, and the authors note the second is unlikely because the biopsies preceded neoadjuvant therapy by weeks to months
critique: The exposed group is six patients and the 83% figure rests on five events, so no precise risk estimate is possible; the interval around 5 of 6 runs from roughly a third to 100%

Reverse causation is not excluded. A transperitoneal aspiration that yields adenocarcinoma marks a tumour bulky and cell-rich enough to hit with a needle, and the finding that none of the nine aspiration-negative patients had peritoneal disease fits tumour biology at least as well as needle seeding

The patient with an equivocal biopsy showing glandular cells, who also had peritoneal metastasis demonstrated at staging, was set aside from the aspiration-positive group; with him the rate is 6 of 7, and the decision to exclude him is an adjudication made with the outcome already known
Table 2's footnote gives P = 0.0001 for the same comparison the abstract and Results report as P = 0.0097

The Discussion gives the no-biopsy group's metastasis rate as 20% overall with 11% peritoneal, where the Results and Table 2 give 8% (14 of 175); five-year survival is 73% in the text and figure and 74% in the abstract
Table 2's denominators of 175, 6 and 9 sum to 190, not the 191 enrolled

The groups are declared similar with P = NS on 6 and 9 patients against 175, where no test could detect a difference; a mass was present in 16% of the aspiration-positive, 36% of the no-biopsy and 66% of the aspiration-negative patients, mean mass size was 3.9 against 2.9 cm, mean age 57 against 50 years, and primary sclerosing cholangitis 17% against 40%

Brush cytology was not performed at all in the aspiration-positive group, so the comparison is between patients diagnosed by needle and patients diagnosed endoscopically, that is between two diagnostic pathways rather than two exposures

Every aspiration was performed at an outside facility, so needle gauge, number of passes, operator and technique are uncontrolled, and 13 percutaneous and 3 EUS-guided procedures are pooled despite differing peritoneal exposure; how many of the three EUS procedures were positive is never stated

Only patients already accepted onto the transplant protocol are counted, so anyone whose outside aspiration took them out of transplant consideration never enters the denominator, and the result cannot be extended to patients being worked up for resection
The interval from aspiration to staging is never reported, only the interval from enrolment to staging, and two patients were staged before enrolment, noted only in a table footnote
No time-to-event analysis and no adjustment for calendar era is attempted across an 18-year span in which protocol criteria, cross-sectional imaging and EUS availability all changed

The 73% five-year survival is reported for the 125 transplanted patients with numbers at risk falling to 33 by five years, and no intention-to-treat figure is given for the 191 enrolled, 66 of whom never reached transplantation
The benchmark used for comparison, a 2.7% needle-track seeding rate after biopsy of hepatocellular carcinoma, is a different endpoint from peritoneal carcinomatosis found at staging laparotomy
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
21492336.n: 191 patients with localised unresectable hilar cholangiocarcinoma enrolled in the Mayo neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and liver transplant protocol between 1 October 1992 and 1 January 2010, of whom 16 had undergone transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration of the primary tumour at an outside facility (13 percutaneous, 3 EUS-guided) and 125 reached transplantation
21492336.bottom_line: This is the paper behind the rule that a hilar mass must not be sampled transperitoneally in anyone who might be a transplant candidate: 5 of 6 protocol patients with a positive outside fine-needle aspiration had peritoneal metastases at operative staging, against 8% of the 175 who had no aspiration. The exposed group is six patients and five events, the comparison is retrospective and unmatched on the histological features that predict peritoneal spread, and a needle that yields adenocarcinoma marks a tumour bulky enough to hit, so reverse causation is not excluded. It also records the Mayo protocol's eligibility rules more explicitly than any other paper in this set, including that pathological confirmation is not required to proceed.
21492336.funding: No funding statement; conflict of interests declared as none

limitations: The study was not a randomised controlled trial, and the authors argue that a trial of transplantation with or without neoadjuvant therapy would be extremely difficult given the rarity of the disease and the unacceptably high recurrence historically reported after transplantation alone

A large proportion of patients came from one centre, 193 of 287, creating a potential for bias, which the authors address by showing no statistical difference in intent-to-treat or recurrence-free survival between that centre and the other 11
Heterogeneity in the duration, type and dose of maintenance chemotherapy across centres meant the independent impact of maintenance chemotherapy could not be determined

Pretransplant surgical staging failed to show a statistical advantage in recurrence-free survival, which the authors attribute mostly to lack of power given that only 30 transplanted patients were unstaged
Because the tumour biology remains incompletely understood, the effect of more rapid access to transplantation is unknown and may raise recurrence in patients whose tumours resist neoadjuvant therapy

Patients without a visible mass on cross-sectional imaging were counted as having a mass smaller than 3 cm for statistical purposes, which the authors state was necessary given the limits of radiographic detection of a small perihilar mass
critique: The headline figures of 78% and 65% recurrence-free survival are measured from the date of transplantation among the 214 patients who reached it; intention-to-treat survival for the 287 enrolled is 68% at 2 years and 53% at 5, and the abstract and conclusion lead with the post-transplant number

71 patients (25%) dropped out at a median of 4.6 months and 60 of the 122 deaths occurred before transplantation, 52 of them from tumour progression; the MELD exception is justified by restating that 25% as an average of 11.5% per 3 months (range 7%-17%) so that it approximates the 10% already assigned to hepatocellular carcinoma

The UNOS/OPTN eligibility criteria being tested were derived from earlier reports by the same group, and are re-evaluated in a dataset in which 193 of 287 patients come from the originating centre, so this is not external validation

The composite 'outside UNOS criteria' exposure, hazard ratio 2.98 (95% CI 1.79-4.95), pools mass over 3 cm (n=21), metastatic disease at transplantation (n=4), direct tumour biopsy (n=16) and prior malignancy within 5 years (n=7); no component is analysed separately, and Figure 4B gives the mass-over-3-cm group as n=23 against n=21 in the text

129 of 287 patients had no mass on imaging and were counted as having a mass under 3 cm, so the mass-size result that drives the selection argument, 5-year recurrence-free survival of 69% against 32%, rests partly on an assumption rather than a measurement

Tissue confirmation at entry was weak: 96 of 287 (33%) had a positive brushing and 65 (23%) a positive biopsy, 75 (26%) were negative on both, and median CA 19-9 was 76 U/mL with only 45% above the 100 U/mL criterion; the authors reduce the number with no proof to 15 (5%) by counting explant pathology and post-transplant recurrence as confirmation, which is evidence obtained after the intervention
Excluding those 15 patients lowers 5-year intention-to-treat survival to 50% and recurrence-free survival to 62%, figures the paper describes as similar to the entire cohort
Living donor allografts are given as 52 in Table 1 and 62 in Supplementary Table 2, where 152 deceased plus 62 living equals the 214 transplanted

The organ cost is absent from the argument for the MELD exception: 214 first grafts plus 22 re-transplantations (10%, eleven of them for arterial compromise) for 287 enrolled patients, in a protocol whose radiation made the portal vein friable in 23% and the hepatic artery in 12%
The 5-year graft survival confidence interval is printed as 60% (95% CI, 68-52), with the bounds reversed

Staging surgery showed no recurrence-free survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.37-1.43) and the timing of staging made no difference (0.79, 0.43-1.43), yet the practice is retained by an indirect calculation applying the 17% metastasis yield to the 30 unstaged patients

Brachytherapy showed no benefit (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.60-1.85) and the authors note that most patients who did not receive it were given a higher external beam dose, so this compares delivery route at similar total dose rather than radiation dose

Centre protocols differ at the level of eligibility, not only therapy: Supplementary Table 1 shows one centre requiring a mass under 2 cm and another admitting masses up to 10 cm, with external beam doses from 2100 to 6000 cGy and brachytherapy from 988 to 5000 cGy, all pooled as one treatment

26 of the 319 reported patients were excluded, including 11 incidental explant diagnoses and 8 transplanted without neoadjuvant therapy, so the group that would form the natural comparator for the value of neoadjuvant therapy is removed from the analysis

Of 50 centres invited, 30 responded and 12 qualified, and the authors identify at least 10 further centres with approved protocols whose outcomes are unknown, so centres with worse results are not represented
Median follow-up was 2.5 years from listing while 5- and 10-year estimates are reported, including 59% (49-69) recurrence-free survival at 10 years, and no numbers at risk appear on any curve
Toxicity is reported without grading or a stated denominator: recurrent clinical or subclinical cholangitis 'occurred in all patients', gastroduodenal ulcers in 34%, nausea or vomiting in 81%
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed; a Covering the Cover synopsis and a CME activity accompany the article and were not reviewed
22504095.n: 287 patients with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma treated under a UNOS-approved neoadjuvant chemoradiation and liver transplant protocol at 12 US centres from January 1993 to July 2010, of whom 214 reached transplantation; 193 of the 287 came from one centre, and 26 patients plus 6 duplicates were excluded from the 319 originally reported
22504095.bottom_line: Across 12 US centres, 214 of 287 patients enrolled in a neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplant protocol reached transplantation and 65% were alive without recurrence at 5 years, which is the evidence base for the standard MELD exception for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Measured from enrolment the same cohort has 53% 5-year survival, 71 patients (25%) dropped out at a median of 4.6 months, and 193 of the 287 came from the centre that wrote the eligibility criteria this study then validates. It establishes that the protocol is reproducible where it is already practised; it does not compare transplantation with resection, cannot isolate any component of the neoadjuvant regimen, and leaves the cost of 236 grafts for 287 patients out of the allocation argument.
22504095.funding: Sarwa Darwish Murad held the 2010/2011 American Association for the Study of Liver Disease/LIFER Clinical and Translational Research Fellowship in Liver Diseases Award; the authors disclose no conflicts

limitations: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is relatively rare so only a few high-quality studies were available, and low-quality studies were included

All the included studies came from a single centre, the Mayo Clinic, which the authors describe as both a weakness and a strength because it limits generalisability while reducing variation in the characteristics of included patients
Some of the same patients are likely to be included in more than one study because all were done at the same centre and the recruitment windows overlap
There is no consensus or criteria for evaluating the quality of diagnostic studies without a control arm, and the studies were classified as high quality on only 10 of the 14 QUADAS items

FISH as a stand-alone test cannot be used either to diagnose cholangiocarcinoma or to exclude a benign stricture, since the positive likelihood ratio for polysomy is 6.81 and the negative 0.56, neither crossing the thresholds of 10 and 0.1
A specificity of 70% for any positive FISH is poor, and a false-positive diagnosis may result in unnecessary treatments and adverse events
FISH increases sensitivity only modestly in primary sclerosing cholangitis, is costly and is not universally available, so its role is confined to cases where brushings are non-diagnostic
Studies from centres other than the one contributing all eight had insufficient patient numbers and were excluded from the analysis
critique: The 'any positive FISH' pool mixes four definitions of a positive test: polysomy alone in two studies, polysomy or trisomy 3 or 7 in three, polysomy plus trisomy or tetrasomy in two, and serial polysomy in one; the table's own footnotes show those same studies yield 47% sensitivity and 100% specificity when only polysomy counts, so the headline 68% and 70% describe no single test

Trisomy and tetrasomy carry a pooled diagnostic odds ratio of 1.28 (95% CI 0.55-2.99) and a positive likelihood ratio of 1.19 (0.65-2.21), that is no diagnostic information at all, and those results sit inside the pool producing the headline figures
Per-study specificity for any positive FISH runs from 52% to 100% in Table 1, with the two largest studies at 73% and 57%, so the pooled 70% conceals the entire usable range

Table 2 shows that specificity differs significantly by population, 0.57 in studies restricted to equivocal cytology against 0.72 in all-indeterminate studies (P less than 0.05), which is a spectrum or threshold effect that argues against pooling them at all

Pooling is by Der Simonian-Laird on sensitivity and specificity separately with a Moses-Shapiro-Littenberg summary curve, which ignores the correlation between the two and the threshold variation dominating this literature; no bivariate or hierarchical model is fitted

The diagnostic odds ratio of 7.24 is interpreted in the Discussion as meaning that with a positive FISH result 'the patient has a 7 times higher chance of having a true pathologic diagnosis', which reads a diagnostic odds ratio as a post-test probability multiplier

Patient-level double counting is conceded but never quantified; the 828 are ERCP episodes at one centre over overlapping periods, so the effective sample size is unknown and the printed confidence intervals are too narrow
Publication bias is declared absent although the Begg-Mazumdar test returned a P value of 0.05, and both bias indicators are uninformative with eight studies
The sensitivity analysis reports the effect of dropping each study on the diagnostic odds ratio and the area under the curve only, not on sensitivity or specificity

Verification bias runs one way: the reference standard is histopathology, and a patient with a positive FISH is more likely to be taken to resection, staging laparotomy or transplantation and so to be classified at all; one included study enrolled patients with a polysomy result and no definitive imaging or pathological evidence of malignancy at the time, so its reference standard is partly later events

The comparator that carries the paper's conclusion, brush cytology at 43% sensitivity and 97% specificity, is quoted from other literature, one source being the same group's concurrent meta-analysis, rather than pooled within this analysis, so the claim that FISH adds little is an indirect comparison

Predictive values are reported at the prevalence of these referral cohorts, a pooled positive predictive value of 42% for any positive FISH and 68% for polysomy, and are never re-derived at the much lower prevalence of a surveillance population, although the paper opens by quoting a 20% lifetime risk

A specificity of 93% for polysomy still means roughly one in fourteen benign primary sclerosing cholangitis strictures tests positive, and polysomy alone can qualify a patient for neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplantation, so the false-positive rate rather than the sensitivity is the decisive number for a tumour board

The practical advice offered is not supported by this analysis: the three-negative-brushings rule placing the probability of malignancy below 6% comes from a 1990 study of 65 patients with bile duct strictures rather than a primary sclerosing cholangitis cohort, and the recommendation against EUS-guided aspiration after negative brushings is justified by the Mayo transplant protocol's exclusion rule, cited to a review
Which 4 of the 14 QUADAS items failed across all studies is shown only in a figure and never stated in the text
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
24360654.n: 828 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis who underwent bile duct brushing with FISH, pooled from 8 full-text studies published to June 2013 and all from a single centre with overlapping recruitment windows; 690 patients in 6 studies contributed polysomy data and 629 in 4 studies contributed trisomy or tetrasomy data
24360654.bottom_line: Pooling eight studies of bile duct brushings in primary sclerosing cholangitis, FISH polysomy is 51% sensitive and 93% specific while any positive FISH is 68% and 70%, which places FISH as an adjunct after a non-diagnostic brushing rather than as a screening test at every ERCP. All eight studies come from one centre with overlapping recruitment, so the same patients are probably counted more than once and this is one institution's experience rather than external validation; the 'any positive FISH' pool also mixes four definitions of a positive result, and trisomy or tetrasomy carries no diagnostic information at all (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.55-2.99). For a tumour board the decisive number is the false-positive rate, since polysomy alone can qualify a patient for neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplantation.
24360654.funding: U. Navaneethan received a research grant from the American College of Gastroenterology; all other authors disclosed no financial relationships relevant to the publication

limitations: The route of preoperative biliary drainage is openly debated, with centres in Asia advocating drainage as mandatory regardless of bilirubin level because of the association between cholangitis and outcome, while others resect undrained patients whose nutritional status is adequate

The role of liver transplantation in resectable de novo hilar disease is not well defined, and in light of the scarcity of donor organs and the absence of superior results with transplantation the panel keeps resection as the standard of care there
The role of adjuvant chemotherapy is still not clearly defined, and the first cooperative group adjuvant trial, SWOG 0809, had results pending at the time of writing
Complete preoperative assessment does not eliminate the risk of non-therapeutic laparotomy or incomplete resection, and 20% to 50% of patients prove unresectable at exploration
A benign aetiology is identified in approximately 10% of resections performed on a presumptive diagnosis of hilar cholangiocarcinoma

The largest study of systemic chemotherapy for advanced biliary malignancy, ABC-02, included a disparate collection of histologies, and the panel adopts it as the best available evidence rather than as hilar-specific evidence
FDG-PET lacks the sensitivity and specificity required of a routine staging tool and rarely adds to the information available from other modalities
Barriers to transplantation include the significant dropout rate during pre-transplant induction therapy and the need for long-term immunosuppression
critique: Nothing is graded. No statement carries a level of evidence or a strength of recommendation, and no methods are described at all: no literature search, no voting procedure, no definition of consensus and no external review, for a document produced by six people at a one-day meeting

The prohibition on percutaneous or laparoscopic biopsy of the primary tumour in potential transplant candidates is referenced to a single study whose exposed group was six patients and whose senior author sits on this panel

The transplant protocol, eligibility rules and survival figures presented as standard of care come from the Mayo programme, which one panel member represents; the statement that transplantation is standard of care for unresectable and PSC-associated disease quotes survival ranges of 55-65% and 35-55% from the start of therapy with no confidence intervals and no dropout rate anywhere in the section

The abstract states that preoperative biliary drainage is best achieved percutaneously, but no consensus statement names a route; the statements list indications only, so the document's most quoted position is not one it formally adopts

That percutaneous preference has not held up: the Coelen randomised trial closed early for excess mortality after percutaneous drainage, and the 2024 Asia-Pacific and 2026 ESGE documents now prefer endoscopic drainage, which also sits awkwardly with this panel's own warning about catheter-tract seeding

The sentence supporting the percutaneous preference reverses its own meaning: the technical success rate measured as time from first attempt to a satisfactory biliary level is reported as 'higher with the endoscopic approach (61 days) than with PTC (44 days)', where a shorter time is the better result
The portal vein embolisation threshold is a future liver remnant below 30% in the abstract and below 30% to 40% in the consensus statement

Resection survival is quoted as 25% to 50% at five years in the resectability section, 27% to 45% for margin-negative resection in the margin paragraph, and 35% to 50% in the summary: three different ranges in one document

Adjuvant chemoradiation is recommended for margin-positive or node-positive disease on retrospective series, one of which showed only that irradiated high-risk patients matched unirradiated low-risk patients (5-year survival 36% against 42%, locoregional recurrence 38% against 37%), which is not a demonstration of benefit, while the Todoroki series assigned adjuvant therapy non-randomly

The only randomised trial cited anywhere in the radiotherapy section enrolled 42 patients and compared percutaneous stenting with brachytherapy and external radiotherapy against stenting alone (median survival 12.9 against 9.9 months), in an era before current systemic therapy
The three criteria that define unresectability are listed without a single supporting citation

The FISH figures of 50% sensitivity and above 95% specificity for polysomy, and the claim that clinical evaluation without FISH predicts malignancy about 90% of the time, are given without pooled sources, and the latter derives from resected patients, that is conditioned on the decision to operate
Systemic therapy is dated by publication: this predates BILCAP, so adjuvant capecitabine is absent, and first-line therapy is gemcitabine-cisplatin from ABC-02, before the chemo-immunotherapy trials

The neoadjuvant regimen called a standardised protocol has itself changed within the experience being cited, the brachytherapy boost having moved from 2000 cGy delivered over 24 hours to 1200-1600 cGy in two to four fractions
Nothing in the document addresses palliative drainage strategy, surveillance after resection, cost or quality of life
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
26172136.n: A six-member expert panel from four institutions, convened by the AHPBA at the January 2014 joint AHPBA/SSAT/SSO/ASCO consensus conference on the multidisciplinary management of bile duct cancer, issuing thirteen ungraded consensus statements; there is no patient cohort
26172136.bottom_line: This is the clearest single statement of the US surgical position on hilar cholangiocarcinoma around 2014: resect the intra- and extrahepatic ducts with the ipsilateral liver and caudate lobe, do not require pathological confirmation first, do not biopsy the primary tumour in a potential transplant candidate, embolise the portal vein below a 30% remnant, and treat unresectable or PSC-associated disease on a standardised neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplant protocol. Nothing in it is graded, no methods are reported, the panel is six people from four institutions meeting for a day, and its percutaneous-drainage preference has since been contradicted by a randomised trial and two later consensus documents. It predates BILCAP and the chemo-immunotherapy trials, so its systemic therapy section should not be used.
26172136.funding: No funding statement; conflicts of interest declared as none

limitations: The study possessed a large degree of heterogeneity, most importantly regarding the index test, which was defined in a variety of ways; positive cytology was not defined in a standard manner across studies
Samples were not uniformly reviewed by blinded reviewers, and in Tischendorf the pathologists were not blinded to the clinical scenario, giving that study a high risk of bias

Only few of the included studies were truly comparative, most evaluating a single modality, so institutional differences in experience and technical expertise limit applicability to smaller or less experienced centres
There is an overall paucity of data: single-operator cholangioscopy, the modality that comes out best, rests on 4 studies and 128 patients

Probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy rests on two studies, one of them a published abstract; publication bias could not be assessed for it, it cannot yield a tissue diagnosis, and the lack of a homogeneous diagnostic standard precludes translating its results into clinical practice
Univariate meta-regression showed that study quality contributed significantly to the heterogeneity of the cholangioscopy estimate

Spectrum bias is possible: in Tischendorf only 8% of patients diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma were alive at the end of follow-up, so cholangioscopy may be more accurate for later-stage disease than for the earlier lesion

Passage of the cholangioscope may be difficult in the narrow strictured ducts of primary sclerosing cholangitis, with 15% procedural failure against 2% in non-PSC controls and 11% post-procedure cholangitis in one included study, and ductal dilation to pass a stricture may cause mucosal trauma that precludes adequate macroscopic evaluation

EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration was excluded because of the tumour-seeding concern and the Mayo transplant protocol's exclusion rule, and because lesion location was not clearly reported in most studies
No cost data were available, and cost-effectiveness analysis is required before a preferred modality can be determined
critique: The headline that cholangioscopy is the most accurate modality at 96% (94-97%) is an accuracy figure, not a measure of discrimination: its pooled sensitivity is 65% (35-87%), indistinguishable from brush cytology's 52% (34-69%) or confocal endomicroscopy's 78% (40-97%), and accuracy in these low-prevalence cohorts is dominated by true negatives, so the ranking is largely a function of prevalence

The accuracy column is internally inconsistent with its own sensitivity and specificity pairs: FISH polysomy at 0.50 and 0.96 is given accuracy 0.69 while brush cytology at 0.52 and 0.99 is given 0.87, and brush cytology's accuracy interval is printed as (0.84-90)

Several intervals in Table 2 do not contain their point estimates: the positive likelihood ratio for brushing plus FISH polysomy is 23.60 (48.30-67.30) and the odds ratio for confocal endomicroscopy plus FISH polysomy is 16 (76-42); FISH trisomy's odds ratio is printed as 1 (1-3)

The abstract gives cholangioscopy's pooled diagnostic odds ratio as 59 (95% CI 10-341) and prints the interval label as '05% CI' in the Results, while Table 2 gives 95 (14-643) for the same comparison

Every combination row, including the conclusion that combining modalities does not improve accuracy over cholangioscopy alone, is imputed from a logistic regression model rather than taken from studies in which both tests were applied to the same patients; that model output is then listed among the paper's strengths
The abstract counts 7 studies on FISH while the Results split them into 7 polysomy and 4 trisomy studies, and the forest plot shows both sets

Cohorts overlap across modalities: Heif 2013 (n=15) contributes to all four, and Charatcharoenwitthaya (n=230), Moreno Luna (n=86) and Shah 2013 to two or three each, so the modality-specific denominators cannot be added and the modalities are partly being compared within the same patients

Eleven of the 21 studies come from one US centre's publication stream, so the cytology and FISH estimates largely recapitulate one institution's experience, as the same authors conceded of their own 2014 FISH meta-analysis

Per-study brush cytology sensitivity in the forest plot runs from 0.07 to 1.00, including two studies at 0.07 and 0.08 and three with a point estimate of 1.00 on one or two true positives; the pooled 0.52 has no clinical referent and the bivariate model's between-study variance is never reported

The Fagan nomogram is run at a pre-test probability of 20%, which is the lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma in primary sclerosing cholangitis rather than the probability at a single ERCP for a dominant stricture, so the quoted 90% post-positive and 9% post-negative probabilities are both overstated for the clinical question

The Discussion concludes that even at low to moderate pre-test probability cholangioscopy should be the recommended confirmatory test, which is a stronger claim than a sensitivity interval of 35% to 87% supports and stronger than the authors' own finding that study quality drove that estimate's heterogeneity

QUADAS-2 is presented only as a grid of symbols with no per-domain tabulation in the text, while the Discussion states that a high risk of bias for the index test was present in a large proportion of studies
The modality the paper recommends is a single-use proprietary platform made by a company for which two of the authors consult, and no cost data were collected

Intraductal biopsy under fluoroscopic guidance, which both the ASGE and ESGE later recommend adding to brushing, was not evaluated, so the comparative-effectiveness claim does not cover the comparator those guidelines favour
No formal organisational guideline existed at the time and no screening strategy is recommended, which the paper notes without resolving
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
27696456.n: 21 studies of ERCP-based tests for cholangiocarcinoma in primary sclerosing cholangitis published to December 2015: 13 of bile duct brushing for cytology (809 patients), 7 of FISH polysomy (701), 4 of FISH trisomy (629), 2 of probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy (66) and 4 of single-operator cholangioscopy with targeted biopsies (128), with several cohorts contributing to more than one modality
27696456.bottom_line: Across 21 studies of ERCP-based tests in primary sclerosing cholangitis, cholangioscopy with targeted biopsy came out with the highest accuracy at 96%, and this is the strongest published case for putting it into the work-up of a dominant stricture. That accuracy is driven by true negatives in low-prevalence cohorts: cholangioscopy's pooled sensitivity is 65% (95% CI 35-87%) on 4 studies and 128 patients, no better than brush cytology's 52%, and the authors' own meta-regression found study quality drove its heterogeneity. The combination estimates, including the claim that combining tests is worse than cholangioscopy alone, are imputed from a regression model rather than taken from patients who had both tests, and the procedure fails in 15% of PSC ducts with 11% post-procedure cholangitis.

limitations: No limitations section beyond two sentences: the authors state that none of the included studies were randomised trials, and then write that 'the negative predictive value is very high, which in the case of a negative test, means that one cannot exclude the disease', which inverts their own finding that the negative predictive value is low
The authors name the location of the lesion as the greatest source of bias in the review, with three studies selecting proximal lesions, one distal, and four not reporting location
Differences in lesion size between studies may have facilitated diagnosis and are named as the other main source of bias, the study with the largest mean lesion size reporting the best results

The authors concede that EUS-guided aspiration does better in distal lesions and ERCP in proximal ones, that lesions under 10 mm and lesions presenting as wall thickening have very low sensitivity by EUS, and that ERCP with cholangioscopy is preferable in those cases
critique: The central comparison is not like with like: the ERCP mean sensitivity of 49% (SD 2.64) comes from the three studies that applied both tests, while the EUS mean of 75% (SD 19.87) comes from all eight, so the headline contrast pools two different evidence bases

The synthesis is an unweighted arithmetic mean of study-level percentages with standard deviations, with no random-effects model, no pooled confidence interval, no I-squared and no bivariate model, although the paper is presented as a meta-analysis performed in RevMan 5.3

Three mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures appear: the per-study tables, the means (79% against 60.66%), and a receiver operating characteristic analysis reporting EUS sensitivity and specificity of 87% and 90% against ERCP's 75% and 81%, figures that appear nowhere else and contradict the 100% specificity reported for EUS in every included study
A fourth pair of figures is produced with an online calculator cited as a reference, giving positive post-test probability and accuracy of 96.5% and 87.7% for EUS and 92.5% and 74.4% for ERCP

Specificity and positive predictive value are 100% for EUS-guided aspiration in all eight studies, that is not one false positive in any cohort; the gold standard is described as histopathology from surgery or from the index test, so the index test can serve as its own reference standard and a false positive is structurally impossible

Rosch 2004 is given identical sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value and accuracy for both tests (46%, 100%, 100%, 60%, 70%), which is implausible for two different tests and reads as one row copied into both

The proximal-stricture studies (DeWitt, Fritscher-Ravens, Nayar) enrolled patients only after ERCP sampling had already failed or been non-diagnostic, which fixes a low ERCP sensitivity by design; the review never stratifies by stricture level despite naming location as its greatest bias
Predictive values are reported at a pooled pre-test probability of 76.66%, with per-study values from 50% to 96%, and are never re-derived at a prevalence a clinician would face
Publication bias is discussed in the abstract sense but never assessed: no funnel plot, no Egger test, no Deeks test

QUADAS-2 is reported narratively with the conclusion that most studies did not impose bias, immediately after naming lesion location as the greatest bias, and no domain-level table appears in the text

The excluded-study list in the PRISMA figure is a free-text block with 50 of 58 full texts excluded, 23 of them labelled review, and includes a citation dated 2985, so the exclusions cannot be audited
The search ends in November 2014 for a paper published online in 2016 and carrying a 2018 citation, so several years of comparative data are missing by the time it appeared

Nothing in the review mentions the central constraint for a hilar patient, that transperitoneal EUS-guided aspiration of the primary tumour disqualifies a candidate under the Mayo transplant protocol and carries a reported peritoneal seeding signal, although Klatskin tumour is one of the paper's keywords
The conclusion recommends EUS-guided aspiration over ERCP for malignant biliary strictures generally, without the location caveat the Discussion itself raises
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
27824027.n: 294 patients from 8 studies of ERCP-based brushing and forceps biopsy against EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration for suspected malignant biliary stricture, searched to November 2014; only 3 of the 8 applied both tests to the same patients and the pooled pre-test probability of malignancy was 76.66%
27824027.bottom_line: This review reports EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration as more sensitive than ERCP brushing and forceps biopsy for a malignant biliary stricture, 75% against 49%, with specificity of 100% in every included study. The comparison is largely indirect: only 3 of 8 studies applied both tests to the same patients, the ERCP figure comes from those three alone, the synthesis is an unweighted mean of percentages, and the three proximal-stricture studies enrolled patients only after ERCP sampling had failed. For a perihilar stricture the usable message is the inverse of the headline, that ERCP sampling is roughly 50% sensitive, that transperitoneal EUS sampling is off-limits in a transplant candidate, which this review never mentions, and that a negative result on either test excludes nothing.

limitations: Detachment atypia, described here, is a close mimic of carcinoma in brushings and accounted for the one benign case called malignant on 7 characteristics

No fixed combination of criteria emerged: requiring chromatin change, nuclear irregularity and pleomorphism together performed worse than any 3 of the 11, and the authors compare this with failed attempts to find criterion combinations in rheumatic fever, Kawasaki disease and papillary thyroid carcinoma
Sensitivity falls as the number of required characteristics rises, so the minimal gain in specificity above three criteria comes at significant cost to sensitivity and accuracy

Well-differentiated tumours can be cytologically bland and extremely difficult to distinguish from benign or reactive change, particularly in primary sclerosing cholangitis, inflammation or prior stenting, which the authors say is partly responsible for the test's low sensitivity
Experience affected performance, with the more experienced reviewers achieving higher specificity and accuracy than the less experienced
A gold standard had to be constructed from reviewer agreement because no independent measure exists of whether a characteristic is present
Abnormal mitoses could not be evaluated at all because no two cytopathologists agreed on their presence in any of the 60 brushings
Features seen infrequently in malignant samples, such as prominent nucleoli at 20% to 28%, are of questionable helpfulness however specific they are
critique: The design is an archival case-control enriched to 50% malignant, so the reported predictive values do not transfer to a clinic population and the 97% specificity rests on 30 selected benign cases

The reference standards are asymmetric: malignancy required histology while benignity required only 18 months of uneventful follow-up; the paper argues against the 6-month standard used elsewhere but gives no justification for 18 months
The single benign case with 7 malignant characteristics was reclassified after the fact as a new entity, detachment atypia, which absorbs the one observation contradicting the rule being proposed

The 3-or-more cut point was selected by scanning all ten cut points in the same 60 cases for the best combination of sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, with no separate validation set, so 70%/97%/83% is a fitted operating point

Three different gold standards were run and the surviving feature list changes with each: at 7 of 7 agreement only 4 of 14 characteristics remain significant, each at exactly P = 0.0384, which indicates a single discordant case driving each

Necrosis is non-significant under the 2-of-3 cytopathologist standard (P = 0.7188) and significant under the 4-of-7 standard (P = 0.0384); the paper's conclusion that necrosis is unhelpful depends on which standard is chosen

Five of the 14 characteristics have no calculable odds ratio because a cell is empty, and three of those, hypercellularity, nuclear molding and prominent nucleoli, are nevertheless listed among the recommended 11 while Table 2 files them under less helpful characteristics
The calculable odds ratios reach 47.46 (95% CI 5.64-399.29) and 50.09 (5.97-420.36), intervals spanning two orders of magnitude on one or zero events in the benign group

Abstract and Table 1 disagree because they draw on different gold standards: three-dimensional clusters are 63% against 3% in the abstract and 52% against 3% in the 2-of-3 cytopathologist column, and nuclear irregularity 70 against 10 rather than 67 against 13
The text reports 22 brushings with 3 or more characteristics of which 1 was benign, while the abstract reports 20 with 4 or more of which 1 was benign; both quote the same single false positive

Six of the seven reviewers are authors of the paper, including the first author, a cytopathology fellow with three months of training who was classed as inexperienced after the results were known, so the interobserver data are not independent of the people who selected the criteria

Seven of 30 malignant brushings had none of the 11 characteristics at the primary gold standard; on blind re-review by all seven reviewers, 3 or more characteristics were found in all 7 cases, so the gold standard for feature presence is not stable on repeat reading of the same slides

No confidence interval is given for any sensitivity, specificity or accuracy figure, although the sample size was set to estimate a sensitivity of 80% with an interval of 70% to 90% and the observed sensitivity is 70%

The malignant cases' primary sites and the strictures' locations are never tabulated, so the proportion that were cholangiocarcinoma rather than pancreatic adenocarcinoma involving the duct, and the proportion that were perihilar, cannot be read; primary sclerosing cholangitis is discussed but no case is identified as such
Individual reviewer sensitivity ranges from 60% to 83% and specificity from 66% to 93%, a spread as wide as the improvement the rule is said to deliver
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
28664934.n: 60 bile duct brushings, 30 malignant with histological confirmation by biopsy (n=6) or resection (n=24) and 30 benign with at least 18 months of uneventful follow-up (15 with and 15 without a prior stent), selected from 253 eligible among 444 archival brushings at one institution over 2000-2015, each read blind by 7 reviewers for 14 malignant characteristics
28664934.bottom_line: Reading a bile duct brushing for eleven defined malignant features and calling it malignant at three or more gives 70% sensitivity, 97% specificity and 83% accuracy, and general surgical pathologists apply the features about as well as cytopathologists do. Those figures come from a 50:50 archival case-control series of 60 cases at one institution, with the cut point chosen by scanning all ten cut points in the same cases, so they are a fitted operating point rather than a validated threshold and the predictive values do not carry over to clinic. No fixed combination of three features worked, a third of cancers are still missed at the recommended threshold, and neither perihilar strictures nor primary sclerosing cholangitis is identified anywhere in the cohort.

limitations: Early termination left a relatively small sample that was underpowered for the primary outcome, so the data should be interpreted with caution
The low patient numbers make the study prone to type I error, which the authors state explicitly of the mortality finding

A third of patients entered after failed or inadequate stenting elsewhere, which might have selected patients at risk of worse outcome and affected the outcome of subsequent procedures, although a sensitivity analysis excluding them showed no difference
No causal relation for the excess mortality was identified by the safety monitoring board or the steering committee, and the cause remains unresolved
Details on bile loss and bile cultures were not collected, reflecting standard care, although they would have been valuable for the hypotheses offered
13% of randomised patients had advanced tumours or benign disease on additional staging after randomisation, which probably affected survival outcomes

The 90-day mortality after resection of 30% is remarkably high against 10% in similar patients treated at the same centres but not recruited during the trial period, which the authors attribute to the high number of extended resections with portal vein reconstruction
critique: The trial was designed to show superiority of percutaneous drainage and powered on an assumed complication rate of 50% endoscopic against 25% percutaneous; the observed rates were 67% and 63%, so the hypothesised effect was absent and the trial was stopped for a harm in the arm it was built to favour

The stopping rule was not prespecified: after the first annual progress report the safety board decided the trial would end if the mortality imbalance increased without a satisfying explanation, with no alpha-spending function and no formal boundary, and the endpoint used was all-cause mortality from randomisation to 90 days after surgery, a window not among the listed secondary outcomes

The 11 deaths in the percutaneous arm include two myocardial infarctions and one progressive disease in patients found unresectable, and one patient with therapy-resistant cholangitis who requested euthanasia, so the stopping decision rests on all-cause mortality rather than on drainage-attributable death

The prespecified primary analysis was a Mann-Whitney U test on the number of complications; the paper reports a Jonckheere-Terpstra test instead (p=0.88), a change made after termination because of the small sample

56% of the endoscopic arm crossed over to percutaneous drainage and crossover was mandatory after two failed endoscopic attempts, so the comparison is of initial strategies and the best-performing arm is in effect endoscopic-first with percutaneous rescue; the post-hoc three-way split gives 9% mortality for endoscopic only, 13% for both routes and 41% for percutaneous only, on 11 to 27 patients per cell

Percutaneous drainage was better on the process measures: technical success 93% against 74% (p=0.07), therapeutic success 78% against 63%, shorter procedure duration and only one crossover; yet bilirubin at two weeks was lower in the endoscopic arm (49 against 100 micromol/L, p=0.04), which is not reconciled with its lower technical success

The baseline table declares the groups similar without a single P value, while C-reactive protein was 10 mg/L (6-19) against 21 (15-32), leucocytes 7.8 against 9.4 x10^9/L and total bilirubin 249 against 280 micromol/L, all higher in the percutaneous arm; none of these was a stratification factor and no analysis adjusts for them
Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group scores were missing for three patients in the endoscopic arm and the printed rows account for only 24 of 27

Percutaneous drains were left in situ postoperatively as transanastomotic drains in 100% of the percutaneous arm against 50% of the endoscopic arm, a difference in postoperative management rather than in preoperative drainage route, and it is not separated from the mortality signal

The percutaneous arm waited 16 days longer for surgery (65 against 49 days, p=0.07) and carried drains 18 days longer (65 against 47 days, p=0.01), an exposure difference that could itself produce progression and deconditioning
Blood loss was 2372 mL in the endoscopic arm against 1450 mL in the percutaneous arm, so the arm with far greater operative blood loss had the lower mortality, and this is not discussed
The 90-day postoperative mortality comparison is relative risk 2.93 (95% CI 0.91-9.55), an interval including 1, and no sample size or power calculation was ever made for a mortality comparison

The 10% mortality in 100 contemporaneous non-trial patients that makes the trial's 26% look anomalous appears only in the appendix with no matching for extent of resection, so the comparison framing the result is itself unadjusted

Three of 23 resection specimens showed benign inflammatory lesions and one further patient was diagnosed with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, so part of the randomised population did not have the disease under study

Of 261 screened only 54 were randomised, and 54 of the excluded patients were excluded because the future liver remnant was already adequately drained, so the trial does not address the common situation of a patient arriving already stented
Enrolment ran 31 months across the four centres that treat most Dutch patients to reach 54, roughly 0.4 patients per centre per month, and no screening log by centre is published

The practical conclusions the authors draw, that drainage should follow resectability assessment at a specialist centre, be selective to the future liver remnant, and may be unnecessary when the remnant exceeds 50% of liver volume, come from Farges and Wiggers and not from anything this trial randomised
A linked Comment (Bridgewater, Webster and Amin, Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018;3:657-58, PMID 30122357) was identified in PubMed but could not be obtained, so no point above draws on it
30122355.n: 54 patients with potentially resectable perihilar cholangiocarcinoma requiring major hepatectomy and with biliary obstruction of the future liver remnant (bilirubin above 50 micromol/L), randomised 1:1 to endoscopic or percutaneous transhepatic drainage at four Dutch academic centres between 26 September 2013 and 29 April 2016, out of 261 screened and against a planned 106; 42 reached exploratory laparotomy and 23 resection
30122355.bottom_line: DRAINAGE is the only completed randomised comparison of endoscopic and percutaneous drainage before resection of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma, and it was negative on its primary endpoint: severe drainage-related complications in 67% of the endoscopic and 63% of the percutaneous arm, relative risk 0.94 (95% CI 0.64-1.40). It was stopped at 54 of 106 patients on an all-cause mortality difference of 41% against 11% that its own authors call prone to type I error and for which no mechanism was found, in a cohort whose overall 90-day mortality was 26% against 10% in contemporaneous non-trial patients at the same centres. With 56% crossover from endoscopic to percutaneous drainage, what the trial compares is an endoscopic-first strategy with percutaneous rescue against primary percutaneous drainage, not the two techniques.

limitations: Data were gathered over an extended period with two generations of cholangioscope, the majority of procedures using the lower-resolution first-generation device, which could have lowered diagnostic accuracy for both visual assessment and targeted biopsies; the authors note that the perceived value of the technique is itself largely based on first-generation studies

Endoscopists and pathologists were not blinded to previous diagnostic results, which could have influenced their assessment of visual features and tissue samples, although the authors would expect non-blinding to raise rather than lower accuracy

A plastic stent was removed immediately before cholangioscopy in 55%, a potential confounder for visual impression, targeted biopsies and brush cytology; the authors believe stent friction produces epithelial change and neovascularisation mistaken for neoplasia, and concede that the same manoeuvre or the biopsies may have raised the yield of the brush cytology taken afterwards

The tertiary referral setting carries a risk of selection bias that could have reduced the apparent accuracy, and the prevalence of primary sclerosing cholangitis at 40% is high, with visual assessment performing worst in that subgroup

A median of three biopsies with 33% inconclusive is the likely explanation for the low biopsy sensitivity; series reporting under 6% inconclusive took at least four biopsies, so the authors recommend a minimum of four, ideally with a pathologist on site
The reference standard allowed only 6 months of benign follow-up, which may misclassify indolent cholangiocarcinoma

No validated criteria for cholangioscopic visual assessment exist, and the criteria for pathological assessment and the processing of targeted biopsies are poorly reported in the comparison literature
The adverse event rate of 13% sits inside a reported range of 2.8% to 21.4% that reflects differences in definition and registration
critique: The three tests are compared on three different and only partly overlapping subsets, visual impression in 80 patients, targeted biopsies in 57 and brush cytology in 58, with no paired statistical test anywhere, so the headline conclusion that brush cytology is superior rests on an unpaired comparison
Biopsy sensitivity is 15% with a 95% interval of 0% to 31%, so it is not distinguishable from nil, and the positive predictive value of 75% rests on 3 true positives and 1 false positive

The intention-to-diagnose analysis counts the 18 inconclusive biopsies (33%) as errors, which is what produces the 65% specificity; excluding them raises specificity to 95.6% while sensitivity reaches only 21.4%, so the headline numbers are driven by specimen failure rather than by misreading, a distinction the conclusion does not preserve

The number of biopsies was recorded in only 43 of 57 patients, so the median of three on which the sampling explanation rests is itself incomplete, and the recommendation of at least four biopsies comes from other series and from a non-significant trend in the 14 second-generation patients

Clinical impact was adjudicated retrospectively from the medical records by a single unblinded reviewer, the first author, against three categories he defined, with no second reviewer and no agreement statistic; the resulting 17% is then set against Chen's 64%, which is a comparison of two differently constructed adjudications

Twenty-six of 80 patients (33%) died during follow-up with no cause given per patient, while benign classification required only 6 months without malignant features, so a patient who died early without resection could be counted benign
Two patients with suspected cholangiocarcinoma but no definitive pathological diagnosis or resection are counted as malignant, so both arms of the reference standard rest partly on clinical judgement
Where the 4 premalignant lesions sit in the 2x2 tables is never stated: the tables use 22 malignant and 58 benign while the aetiology table lists 22 malignant plus 4 premalignant

Neovascularisation, the feature the authors identify as most affected by stents, is reported descriptively (12 of 22 malignant, 16 of 58 benign) with no accuracy calculation and no statistical test of the stent association (20 of 28 patients with neovascularisation had a stent removed, against 24 of 52 without)

The two explanations the paper offers for its negative result, the primary sclerosing cholangitis subgroup and the second-generation device, are both in supplementary tables, as are the likelihood ratios, so neither can be checked against the published text

Table 4 sets this study's 64%/62% and 15%/65% against twelve prior series reporting visual sensitivity of 78% to 100% and biopsy sensitivity of 43% to 88%, but several of those series do not state their primary sclerosing cholangitis prevalence and one excluded it, so the comparison that frames this result as an outlier is not matched on the variable the authors blame

Over 11 years, 86 cholangioscopies for this indication were performed by three endoscopists, roughly eight a year for the whole unit, and no per-operator results are given for a procedure the paper itself says requires expertise

A cardiac arrest during cholangioscopy followed by a stroke is counted inside the 13% adverse-event total but sits outside the three events labelled serious, so the stated serious-event rate of 4% excludes the most severe event recorded

Both false-positive brush cytology results occurred in non-PSC patients with a plastic stent removed before the procedure, that is by the same mechanism the authors invoke to explain cholangioscopy's false positives, and the comparator is nonetheless presented as superior

Cost is quoted at 4680 euros per patient from a single external reference with no local costing and no cost-effectiveness analysis, while the conclusion advises against adopting the technique as standard of care
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed
31858509.n: 80 patients with indeterminate biliary strictures who underwent single-operator peroral cholangioscopy at one Dutch tertiary centre between November 2007 and September 2018, from 185 cholangioscopies and 86 performed for that indication: 32 (40%) with primary sclerosing cholangitis, 36 (45%) with hilar strictures and 22 (28%) with a malignant final diagnosis; targeted biopsies were taken in 57 and brush cytology performed in 58
31858509.bottom_line: In 80 patients with indeterminate strictures, 40% of them with primary sclerosing cholangitis and 45% hilar, single-operator cholangioscopy performed worse than the brush cytology taken at the same procedure: visual impression 64% sensitive and 62% specific, targeted biopsy 15% and 65%, brush cytology 47% and 95%, and the result changed management in 17%. The low biopsy figure is largely specimen failure rather than misreading, since 33% of biopsies were inconclusive on a median of three and excluding them raises specificity to 95.6% while sensitivity reaches only 21.4%, and the three tests were computed on three different overlapping subsets with no paired comparison. It is the strongest published warning that cholangioscopy's reported accuracy, most of it from first-generation devices in cohorts with little primary sclerosing cholangitis, does not transfer to a stented PSC population.
31858509.funding: No funding statement; the authors declare that they have no conflict of interest, and no additional institutional review board permission was required because the study was retrospective

limitations: All three recommendations are conditional and rest on low quality evidence, and the panel closes by listing the trials that would be needed in each area

The existing randomised trials of metal against plastic stents did not schedule regular plastic stent exchanges but waited for occlusion, which the panel names as the major limitation in answering its first question; future trials should compare metal stents against regularly replaced plastic stents to mirror practice
Evidence on survival and stent patency was rated down for imprecision because of the assumption of normality when pooling medians, and much of it came from single studies
The term bilateral stent placement is the wrong frame; future studies should use multisectoral stent placement, meaning right anterior, right posterior and left main duct

No studies reporting patient values were found for the stent-type question, so the panel relied on discussion with the patient advocate and its own assumption that patients would value survival and fewer reinterventions
There are no true cost-effectiveness analyses in the United States, and the one cost-effectiveness study of endoscopic against percutaneous drainage comes from Thailand with limited generalisability

Two of the three randomised trials of endoscopic against percutaneous drainage ended early, the Dutch trial for higher early mortality and the only US trial for prohibitively slow accrual, and the evidence was rated down for risk of bias on that account
The general concept statements, including those covering the transplant candidate, are expert opinions of the panel for which no systematic review was conducted
critique: Recommendation 2 favours bilateral stenting although almost every outcome examined was null or ran the other way: technical success was significantly lower for bilateral placement (odds ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.17-0.91), drainage success did not differ (1.0, 0.36-2.76), early and late adverse events did not differ, late stent occlusion did not differ, pooled survival did not differ (11 days, -12 to 35) and pooled patency did not differ (standardised mean difference 0.38, -0.22 to 0.99, I-squared 78%); the recommendation rests on two adjusted hazard ratios from a single randomised trial

Pooled survival and patency effects are computed as standardised mean differences from reported medians, patient numbers and P values on an assumption of normality that the panel itself rated the evidence down for, while continuing to use the estimates

Several reported P values contradict their intervals: pancreatitis after endoscopic against percutaneous drainage is given as odds ratio 3.69 (1.20-11.33, P = .22), and overall adverse events (1.8, 1.03-3.13) and cholangitis (2.04, 1.00-4.14) are described as not reaching significance although their intervals exclude or touch 1; insertion success for metal against plastic stents is 6.38 (0.86-47.45)

34023067.bottom_line: The ASGE's three conditional recommendations for malignant hilar obstruction are metal or plastic stents for palliation with metal preferred where repeated intervention is to be avoided, bilateral rather than unilateral stenting when the liver is not atrophic, and against routine percutaneous drainage as first-line therapy before resection. Every recommendation rests on low quality evidence, and the bilateral-stent recommendation is made although technical success was significantly lower with bilateral placement and pooled survival, patency, drainage success and adverse events all showed no difference; the case against percutaneous drainage rests on a seeding meta-analysis the panel itself grades very low (7.8% against 17.1%, I-squared 66%). 37307900.bottom_line: The ASGE's three conditional recommendations, all on very low quality evidence, are to add fluoroscopy-guided biopsy to brush cytology, to use cholangioscopy-guided biopsy in non-distal strictures where the critical liver segment can be drained, and to add EUS after a non-diagnostic ERCP or for a distal stricture, with the explicit practice point that the hilar mass itself must not be punctured in a potential transplant candidate. Heterogeneity runs to I-squared of 80% to 90% for the central estimates, EUS alone and ERCP alone do not differ in sensitivity, and every forest plot and evidence profile sits in a separate companion article. Even the best combination leaves sensitivity at 0.66 to 0.88, so a negative endoscopic work-up excludes nothing, and primary sclerosing cholangitis is left to a future-directions list.

39285860.n: 24 experts in hepatobiliary endoscopy, gastroenterologists and surgeons, from 14 countries in the Asia-Pacific region, voting anonymously in two modified Delphi rounds on statements drafted from a three-database literature search, producing 7 statements and 5 key concepts; there is no patient cohort
39285860.bottom_line: The updated Asia-Pacific consensus gives a workable endoscopic algorithm for malignant hilar obstruction: combine intraductal biopsy and cytology at the index ERCP, drain more than 50% of viable liver with the stent number set by Bismuth type and sector volume, select the segment by guidewire under pre-defined imaging with air or carbon dioxide cholangiography, and use EUS-guided or percutaneous drainage as rescue. The perihilar brushing-plus-biopsy recommendation pools two retrospective cohorts of 58 and 43 patients, reports I-squared of 0% from two studies, and the second of those used a double-balloon enteroscopy forceps advanced through a plastic pusher after guidewire removal, a technique most units do not have

The strongest evidence in the perihilar section, a multicentre randomised trial of more than 400 patients in which cytology sensitivity rose from 38% to 47% to 57% with 10, 20 and 30 brush passes, appears only in the discussion text and is not made a recommendation

Cost-effectiveness is quoted from single studies in unnamed health systems in both dollars and euros and applied across European practice with no sensitivity analysis
